requirement.title: Destructive maintenance over MCP requires an explicit capability grant
requirement.body: Destructive maintenance tools exposed over MCP default to preview-only. They perform destructive work in exactly one condition: an explicit out-of-band capability grant is present in the server environment. Transport kind is excluded from the authority decision, because a proxy can front a local stdio pipe with a shared network surface, so a transport reported as local is uninformative about caller identity. When the grant is absent, the tool returns a preview result whose message names the required grant and the equivalent command-line invocation. The command-line entry point applies its own caller's arguments directly, since that caller already holds local shell authority.

The server runs as a stdio subprocess behind a shared proxy
scenarios.when: A client requests a destructive run
then: The tool performs a preview-only run
The response reports that the destructive run was refused
The response names the required grant and the command-line equivalent

scenarios.title: Explicit grant authorizes the destructive run
given: The capability grant is present in the server environment
scenarios.when: A client requests a destructive run
then: The tool applies the caller's requested mode

scenarios.title: Command-line path stays independent of the grant
scenarios.when: An operator runs the destructive command-line invocation with the execute flag
then: The reported outcome matches the operator's requested mode

requirement.title: Candidate lookup reports distinct filters, visible truncation, and result freshness
requirement.body: Candidate reference lookup MUST make its declared usage filters observably distinct. A filter that promises to include test occurrences MUST return test occurrences when they exist, even when production occurrences alone would exceed the result cap. Responses MUST report how many production and test occurrences matched and how many of each were returned, so truncation is visible rather than inferred. Each returned occurrence MUST carry a freshness indicator derived from comparing the backing file's current content against the indexed content, and the response MUST summarise how many backing files were stale. A backing file that no longer exists MUST be reported as stale rather than raising an error. Freshness is reported, never repaired: lookup MUST NOT re-index as a side effect. Freshness work MUST be bounded by the returned result slice, not by repository size.

then: The response contains at least one test occurrence
The response differs from the production-first response for the same query

scenarios.title: Truncation is reported

then: The response reports the number of matching production and test occurrences

scenarios.title: Stale occurrences are flagged and recoverable
given: The file is then modified so its content no longer matches the index
scenarios.when: The caller runs a lookup returning occurrences from that file
then: The response summarises the count of stale backing files

documents.proposal:
# Fix lookup and prune defects

## Intent

Close the three defects that managed-endpoint validation proved reach agents: an ineffective destructive-tool guard, a usage filter that does nothing, and silently stale results.

## Root Cause Analysis

### Defect 1 — destructive prune guard is defeated by proxy deployment

`_transport_is_local` in `src/lgrep/server/tools_maintenance.py:57-81` returns true when the transport string is `stdio`, on the stated assumption that stdio is "single-user and inherently access-controlled (the caller is the same process tree as the server)". Vision runs lgrep as a stdio subprocess but publishes it on a shared HTTP port that any local client can reach, and no bearer token is configured. Diagnostics requested through that HTTP session report `transport: "stdio"`, so the guard grants full destructive rights to a shared surface. The root cause is that transport kind was used as a proxy for caller trust; that inference breaks the moment a multiplexing proxy fronts the pipe.

### Defect 2 — `include_tests` is a dead branch

In `src/lgrep/tools/search_references.py:119-136` the `production_first` and `include_tests` branches apply byte-identical sort keys and neither filters. Both therefore return the same ordering and the same total. Because production occurrences sort first and the response is capped, test occurrences fall past the cap and are unreachable through `include_tests`. Empirically both filters returned 133 total matches, 100 rows, and zero test hits, while `tests_only` returned 5 test rows. The root cause is that the filter was specified as three modes but implemented as two, with no test covering the difference between them.

### Defect 3 — stale occurrences carry no freshness signal

`search_references` reads persisted occurrence rows and returns their stored `line_number` and `line_text` without comparing them to the file on disk. After shifting a fixture module's lines without re-indexing, 21 returned rows pointed at wrong lines while the response remained well-formed and carried only the generic candidate disclaimer. The root cause is a missing freshness check at query time even though the index already stores a per-file SHA-256 hash, used today only to skip unchanged files during incremental indexing.

## Scope

`src/lgrep/server/tools_maintenance.py`, `src/lgrep/tools/search_references.py`, the occurrence response model in `src/lgrep/server/responses.py`, and their tests. Documentation and changelog accompany the behavior changes.

## User outcomes

- Destructive maintenance cannot be triggered from a shared proxied surface without deliberate, explicit opt-in.
- Asking for test usages actually returns test usages.
- A result that may be out of date says so, instead of looking authoritative.

## Constraints

- Preserve the candidate-only contract: results stay advisory, never claimed exhaustive or compiler-accurate.
- Keep the local CLI able to perform real deletions.
- Keep query latency well inside the existing per-request budget.
- No migration of the MCP SDK and no unrelated dependency upgrades.
documents.problemStatement:
Managed-endpoint validation of lgrep found three defects that reach agents directly. Destructive prune tools are reachable without their intended guard because the guard trusts the stdio transport while Vision fronts that same stdio subprocess with a shared unauthenticated HTTP port. The `include_tests` usage filter returns results identical to `production_first`, so it cannot surface test occurrences once the result cap truncates the response. Candidate occurrences from an outdated index are returned with correct-looking line numbers and text and no freshness signal, so agents cannot tell a current hit from a stale one.</problemStatement>

# Agreement — Fix lookup and prune defects

## Objective

Make destructive maintenance safe on shared deployments, make the usage filters mean what their names say, and stop presenting stale occurrences as current.

## Acceptance criteria

- **AC1 — Destructive rights require explicit grant:** transport kind alone never authorizes destructive maintenance through MCP. Without an explicit opt-in the destructive tools coerce a preview-only run and say why, including when the transport reports itself as local.
- **AC2 — Opt-in and CLI still work:** with the explicit opt-in present, destructive MCP calls perform real work, and the local CLI destructive path is unchanged.
- **AC3 — Filters are observably distinct:** for one query over a corpus whose test occurrences fall beyond the result cap, the three usage filters return three different result sets, and asking to include tests actually returns test occurrences.
- **AC4 — Truncation is visible:** responses report how many production and test occurrences matched and how many were returned, so a caller can tell that results were cut off.
- **AC5 — Staleness is signalled:** when a returned occurrence comes from a file whose current content no longer matches the indexed content, the response marks that result stale and summarises how many files were stale; re-indexing clears the marks; a deleted file is treated as stale rather than as an error.
- **AC6 — Contract and budget preserved:** results remain explicitly candidate-only, and a capped query against a fixture with stale files stays well inside the existing per-request time budget.
- **AC7 — Proven end to end:** the full test suite and lint pass, and the three fixed behaviors are reproduced through the real Vision-managed endpoint.

## Constraints

- Do not migrate the MCP SDK and do not upgrade unrelated dependencies.
- Do not modify Vision configuration, topology, or ports.
- Keep freshness checking bounded to the files actually returned.
- Preserve the existing response fields that callers already depend on; additions only.

## Out of scope

- Automatic re-indexing on detected staleness.
- Authentication for the Vision proxy itself.
- Extending reference lookup beyond Python or beyond candidate semantics.
documents.design:
# Design — Fix lookup and prune defects

## 1. Destructive rights become an explicit capability

Delete the transport-trust inference. A transport string cannot prove who the caller is once a proxy multiplexes the pipe, which is exactly how Vision runs lgrep.

Replace it with an explicit environment opt-in, defaulting to off. When the opt-in is absent, destructive maintenance tools force preview mode and return a reason naming the opt-in and the CLI alternative. When present, they honour the caller's argument. The CLI path does not consult the opt-in, because the CLI caller already has local shell authority.

This is deliberately fail-closed: the previous behavior granted destructive rights by default in the one deployment that most needed protection.

## 2. Usage filters get distinct, honest semantics

Keep `production_first` exactly as it behaves today so existing callers are unaffected: production occurrences first, tests after, truncated at the cap.

Give `include_tests` a reserved slice. Compute the test-occurrence set separately, reserve up to a fixed minority share of the cap for test rows when tests exist, fill the remainder with production rows, then present production first. When there are fewer tests than the reserve, the unused reserve returns to production, so no capacity is wasted.

Add explicit counts to every response: how many production and test occurrences matched, and how many of each were returned. Truncation becomes visible rather than inferred, which is what made the original defect invisible.

`tests_only` is unchanged.

## 3. Staleness is computed at query time

The symbol index already stores a per-file SHA-256 used to skip unchanged files during incremental indexing. Reuse it as the freshness oracle instead of adding new state.

After the result slice is chosen, hash the distinct files backing those results and compare against the stored hashes. Mark each result from a mismatched file as stale, and summarise the count on the response. A file that no longer exists is stale, not an error. Work is bounded by the number of returned rows, never by repository size, which keeps the check inside the request budget.

Freshness is reported, never repaired. Automatic re-indexing stays out of scope so a read-only lookup keeps no write side effects.

## Verification

Drive each defect with a failing test first, since all three were invisible precisely because no test distinguished the behaviors. Then re-run the managed-endpoint matrix used to find them and confirm the three responses now differ, stale rows are flagged, and the destructive tools refuse without the opt-in.
documents.executiveSummary:
# Executive Summary — Fix lookup and prune defects

## Outcome

Three defects found by managed-endpoint validation of the previous change are fixed and proven over the real MCP protocol.

**Deleting through the shared service now requires an explicit grant.** The two destructive maintenance tools decided whether a caller was allowed to delete by looking at the transport kind, treating `stdio` as proof of a single trusted local user. That inference was wrong in exactly the deployment that most needed protection: the shared service runs lgrep as a local subprocess but republishes it on an unauthenticated port, and the subprocess still reports `stdio` — so any client that could reach the port could delete indexed data. Authority is now an explicit server-side opt-in that defaults to off. Without it the tools return a preview and state which grant or which command-line equivalent would be needed. The command-line path, whose caller already holds local shell authority, is unchanged.

**The reference-lookup filters now mean what their names say.** Asking to include test occurrences returned none, because production occurrences alone filled the result cap before any test occurrence was considered. A fifth of the cap is now held for test occurrences, with unused capacity handed back to the other group, so the three filter modes produce three genuinely different result sets.

**Truncated and stale results now say so.** Responses report how many production and test occurrences matched versus how many were returned, so a caller can tell results were cut off instead of inferring it. Each result is marked stale when its source file has changed since indexing, with a per-response count of stale files; a deleted file is reported as stale rather than raising an error. Freshness reuses a fingerprint the index already stores, so no re-reading of the repository is involved and the check costs nothing beyond the rows actually returned.

## Why it matters

The first fix closes a data-loss exposure on a shared service. The other two close a subtler failure: the tool was answering confidently with results that were incomplete or out of date, and gave the caller no way to notice. Silent wrongness is more expensive than visible wrongness, because it is acted on.

## Verification

- Full test suite: **719 passed**; lint and format checks clean across the whole repository.
- All four tasks followed a failing-test-first cycle with recorded red and green runs.
- Ten behavioural scenarios exercised over real JSON-RPC against a clean build of the change branch: **all pass**, slowest request 0.023s against an 8-second budget.
- Independent review across security, correctness, and contract traceability. Contract coverage 100% — all 14 items traced, every diff hunk attributable.

## Release Readiness Summary

Hardening found documentation drift and a pre-existing continuous-integration failure, both now fixed.

**Documentation contradicted the shipped behaviour.** Two specification documents and the README still instructed readers that the transport kind decides deletion rights — the exact rule this change removes. A dated audit document had also recorded that rule as a *positive* security finding. The specs and README are rewritten; the audit entry is annotated as superseded rather than edited, because the mistaken finding is itself the lesson: it verified that a guard existed without checking what the guard actually discriminated on, and that false reassurance delayed discovery.

**Continuous integration was already failing before this change.** The lint job had been red on the main branch, caused by an unpinned formatter dependency: the build installed a newer version than contributors run, which changed its formatting choices and additionally began formatting code examples embedded in Markdown. The formatter is now pinned to a compatible range so the build and local development cannot silently diverge again, Advance's own state directory is excluded from formatting, prose files are excluded so hand-wrapped examples survive, and the affected source files are formatted. This repair was outside the change's contract and was approved by the user before being applied.

## Risks and follow-ups

- **Managed re-verification is a post-merge step.** The shared service must run an artifact built from the merged main branch, so pre-merge proof was taken over the same local subprocess channel the service itself spawns. Re-running the scenario matrix through the managed endpoint after merge is the confirming step.
- **The prior change remains parked at acceptance** with one criterion recorded as failed — the very defects this change fixes. It needs a decision once this merges.
- The grant is a capability flag, not caller authentication. Anyone who can set the service's environment can enable deletion. Authenticating the proxy itself was explicitly out of scope.

## Review findings

Nine findings, no blockers; six fixes applied during remediation. The substantive one: the staleness annotation was writing its verdicts into the shared cached index rather than into copies, which would have leaked read-only query state into indexed data on the next save — a violation of this change's own scope boundary that the original tests did not catch. Also fixed: the freshness read was not confined to the repository root and could follow an absolute path outside it; a malformed path would have raised an uncaught error type and failed the whole lookup; and two specification documents still mandated the transport rule this change removes.

clarify_findings.message: Proposal describes behavior that could fail but doesn't mention error handling or rollback. What happens when things go wrong?

release_notes.headline_internal: Replace transport-inference destructive authority with LGREP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE_MCP grant; add reserved-slice include_tests, match/return counts, and per-result staleness
release_notes.headline_external: Deleting through the shared lgrep service now requires an explicit opt-in, and reference lookup reports truncation and staleness
highlights: Destructive MCP maintenance (prune_orphans, prune_symbols) now defaults to preview-only and deletes only when LGREP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE_MCP is set on the server. Transport kind no longer grants authority — a proxy can front a local stdio pipe with a shared port. Refused calls return refused_reason naming the grant and the CLI equivalent.
include_tests now returns test occurrences: a fifth of the result cap is reserved for them, with unused reserve handed back to production.
Reference responses report production_matches, test_matches, returned_production, and returned_tests, so truncation is visible rather than inferred.
Each result carries is_stale, and responses carry stale_file_count, computed from the per-file SHA-256 the index already stores. A deleted backing file is reported stale rather than raising.

breaking.description: Destructive MCP prune calls that previously succeeded over a stdio transport now return a preview instead of deleting.
breaking.migration: Set LGREP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE_MCP in the server environment to restore destructive MCP behaviour, or use the CLI equivalents (lgrep prune-orphans --execute, lgrep prune-symbols --execute), which are unaffected.

worker_bundle_impact.rationale: lgrep is a Python MCP server and CLI. The repository contains no ADV Temporal worker bundle, no workflow code, and no replay-determinism surface. The diff is confined to src/lgrep/, tests/, docs/specs/, CHANGELOG.md, README.md, and pyproject.toml.
